subtitle: How I filtered 8,234 companies into a long-term ETF portoflio
title: StockTok ETF
description: How I filtered 8,234 companies into a long-term ETF portoflio
body_html:
James asked for this post…and I am happy that he did. After reviewing 8234 stocks, I made a surprising discovery about the finance sector. My speculation is that we are going to have some big stock performers in finance in the coming months. I have alerts set, so be ready and stay tuned as I pick up those positions over time. Now, onto the ETF construction.

The first thing I want to do is narrow my list to only high-growth-potential assets. Think about it. A stock like Nvidia, at roughly a $4.5 trillion market cap, has very limited growth potential. Even if that stock doubled in market cap, which is extremely unlikely, that would only result in a 100% gain. The odds of that happening are close to zero. A near-zero chance at a 100% return does not make sense from an investing standpoint.

Now compare that to a $1 billion market-cap company. The upside potential is materially different. These companies have a realistic path to doubling, tripling, or more. Yes, there are many stocks to choose from, but this approach is far more logical than targeting assets with limited upside. The first step is simply creating a list of candidates. By doing this, the universe is reduced from 8,234 stocks to 2,754. There will be long-term winners in this group.

Normally, when I am mid-term trading, I want companies that are blowing out earnings, generating significant cash flow, and posting strong EPS. But some of these companies may not be profitable yet. That is fine. At a minimum, they need to have cash flow. Any cash flow at this stage matters.

This filter is simple. I required trailing 12-month free cash flow to be greater than 1. That alone eliminated another 815 companies, reducing the list to 1,939.

The best indicator in the stock market is price action. Some companies may look great on paper, but the stock price never goes up. That is a harsh truth. I see this all the time. People say a company is great, but when you look at the chart, the stock is just trending lower.

Since this is a long-term approach, I want to see strength on higher time frames, specifically the monthly chart. To keep things simple, I set a clear rule: price must be above the 12-month moving average. Trend is your friend. I also prefer this because it ensures the company has been publicly traded for at least one year. This rule eliminated another 808 stocks, bringing the list down to 1,131.

This is still too many stocks to work with. We need to get the list down to roughly 300 or fewer so it becomes manageable to review manually. I will not bore you with those details here.

To get there, I applied a few simple filters. First, I limited the list to stocks in the Russell 2000 or the S&P 500. This gives us recognizable companies and increases the likelihood that institutions are already paying attention to them. Next, I removed stocks with extremely low price-to-earnings ratios. At this stage, the goal is simply to eliminate obvious duds. Valuations can expand later, but there is no reason to start on the wrong foot.

These two filters reduced the list to 633 companies.

The final filters are more about preference than anything else. I excluded stocks trading below $10, as they are less likely to attract institutional interest. I also removed stocks priced above $750, since splits tend to become more common at those levels. This is a very wide parameter.

I also prefer companies with more than 20 employees. Finally, beyond simply having cash flow, I want to see cash flow that is growing. These filters reduced the list to 333 companies.

If we cannot find 10 winners out of 333, we have bigger problems.

You already know I am a big fan of volatility contraction patterns (VCP). They show up on every time frame, including the monthly. I went through all 333 charts. Yes, it took about an hour. On each one, I asked a simple question: does this meet the basic requirements of a macro volatility contraction pattern? Only 30 charts did.

If you are not familiar with VCPs, the idea is straightforward. Price trends higher, forms higher lows, and volatility contracts as volume declines. That is the type of long-term setup I am looking for.

And this part genuinely surprised me.

When I started this project, I did not expect the final ETF to be so heavily weighted toward the financial sector. But after reviewing the charts, the results were clear. Of the 30 remaining candidates, 22 showed strong volatility contraction patterns in finance-related names.

That concentration was not intentional. It was purely the outcome of the rules. Many of these charts, I have set alerts for to buy myself.

Below are the 10 stocks I would assemble to build this ETF today.

This ETF was required to have 10 stocks, so at this point we can manually narrow the list further. Since this is a long-term hold, I only want companies with improving financials on an annual basis. As I worked through the finance sector, I focused on firms with stable businesses, consistent profitability, and shareholder-friendly behavior.

At the end of the day, it comes down to shareholders getting paid. Companies that consistently make money and return value tend to attract capital. These four fit that criteria:

  • Prudential Financial,

  • M&T Bank,

  • Simon Property Group,

  • United Bankshares,

Because this is an ETF, I did not want it to be overloaded with financial stocks. A black swan or catalyst in the sector could decimate the ETF. That left eight remaining candidates that met all requirements: TXT, HNI, SPB, CAKE, ACEL, FDX, MSCI, and VLO.

We only needed to eliminate two to complete the 10-stock ETF. Similar to the financial sector, I removed the names that did not show consistent annual improvement in EPS. CAKE and ACEL were eliminated.

So the final list for the 10 stock StockTok ETF:

  • Textron Inc,

  • HNI Corporation,

  • Spectrum Brands Holdings, (this is probably my least favorite on the list)

  • FedEx Corporation,

  • MSCI Inc,

  • Valero Energy Corporation,

You may be asking: “Well how do some of these hold up fundamentally through 2026 or 2027?”

I have no idea…narratives change. What I do know is they meet all of our requirements:

  • They are making money, many at a stable rate. At least the shareholders are.

  • The trend is up on the long term scale. Trend is friend.

  • They all show volatility contraction patterns.

You might be asking, “How do these hold up fundamentally through 2026 or 2027?”

I do not know. Narratives change. What I do know is that every name on this list meets the same requirements:

  • They are making money, often at a stable rate. At the very least, shareholders are getting paid.

  • The long-term trend is up. Trend is your friend.

  • They all show clear volatility contraction patterns
